description: A solo team building a tool for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge: compare candidate south pole landing sites and dates by how long the Sun and Earth stay above the horizon, so planners can judge solar power and direct-to-Earth communication at a glance. The team is complete and is not looking for new members.
summary: Lunar missions slip, and at the south pole a slip decides whether a lander gets sunlight for its batteries and a line of sight to Earth. The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser tool that compares up to five landing sites and dates over real NASA LRO terrain, using Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons. It shows how long each site stays dark, how much Earth link it gets, and a new slip-margin map: how many days a landing can slip at every 1 km point near the pole. With a 60 h battery and a 40% link need, a 7-day mission from 24 June 2027 can slip 12 days at the best point, and no point absorbs two weeks.
details: The Navigator answers that in a browser with nothing to install. Pick a landing date, a mission length, how many hours of darkness the battery can bridge, and how much Earth link the mission needs. For up to five of 22 sites it shows a year of landing days as a line of light: gold is the Sun, blue is the Earth link, and ink marks the days a landing works. A horizon panorama shows the real LRO terrain skyline with the Sun and Earth crossing it. A new slip-margin map tries every landing day at every 1 km point within 100 km of the south pole and keeps the longest unbroken run that meets your limits.Result: with a 60 h battery and a 40% link need, a 7-day mission from 24 June 2027 can slip at most 12 days at the best point, 2,743 km2 work on the exact date, and no point absorbs a slip of two weeks.Validation: Sun and Earth positions were checked at 600 random moments against live JPL Horizons (worst error 0.00003 degrees). Limits: sunlight and line of sight only (no heat, dust or slope); terrain exists only south of 80 S, so other sites assume a flat horizon; not tested on a physical phone, Safari or Firefox.Super Intelligence use: Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote most of the code and design under the team's direction. The demo video narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs); a captions-only version is also provided. All figures are computed from NASA data and covered by checks.
